name: Iris Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My week is a mix of media and sociology lectures, a group project on how people use food delivery apps, and a lot of coffee. I live in a flat share above a chip shop with two friends from my course. On the side I run the Instagram for a café called Brew and Bloom, which pays 120 a month and a free flat white a day. I use AI tools constantly, for notes, captions, planning my week, everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine, it's a useful tool and everyone calming down is healthy. I'd still keep using it every day, because even a modest tool saves me an hour on captions. I'd probably make a funny post about the doom videos I watched in 2025.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be pretty relaxed. My parents split when I was ten, and Mum's a nurse, so I grew up knowing money is tight in a normal world, not just an AI one. A boring world is one I know how to live in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with Brew and Bloom and try to get two more small clients, a florist and a gym. I'd keep my loan under control and aim to save 50 a month. And I'd keep learning the tools anyway, because being quick with them is a skill even if the hype is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. I like the buzz of a big change, so there's a tiny disappointment. But a quiet world is a kind world to a student on a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said money is tight even in a normal world. What's the tightest bit right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent after the family help runs out in June. Mum gives me 150 a month and I've got 120 from the café and a few shifts. If the café closed, I'd lose a fifth of my income overnight, and small cafés do close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a second small client early, so one loss doesn't hurt. I've already sent a message to a bookshop on my road offering to run their page for free for a month. The point of offering a bookshop a free month isn't the free month, it's the testimonial for the next client.

say: I'd say everyone calming down is **healthy**, and keep using the tools.
I'd post a joke about the **doom videos** from 2025.
think: A boring world is one I **know** how to live in.
My real risk is **money**: the café could close and take a fifth of my income.
do: **Win** two more small clients, like a florist and a gym.
**Save** 50 a month from the freelance money.
feel: **Calm** and a little flat, because I like big change.
**Safe**, though aware that small cafés do close.
S0.quote: The point of offering a bookshop a free month isn't the free month, it's the testimonial for the next client.
fieldNote: Her **side-income** instinct appears even when nothing is wrong.
Calm on AI, but money is genuinely thin: 120 from the café is a fifth of her income.
Treats upheaval with appetite; the quiet world mildly disappoints her.

steps.text: Offer a bookshop a free month of social media work
Save 50 a month from the freelance pay
Use AI tools daily to cut caption time
Keep running the café's Instagram page

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's exciting and scary in about equal parts. I'd post about it, because that's what I do, and probably get a hundred comments. I'd also say that caption writing and basic design are what's going first, so freelancers like me have to be more than a pair of hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's what I do. Captions, scheduling, simple copy for local businesses, that's the stuff the tools do better each month. In three years a café can ask the tool, for free, and not pay me 120.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move from doing the posts to doing the strategy: the photos, the voice, the events, the things that need someone local. I'd learn video editing and basic analytics. I'd also ask my tutor about work in research or communications for charities, which I think values people who understand what's happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired. A bit like standing at the top of a slide, and not sure whether it's fun. I also feel a bit of embarrassment, as if I'm using the thing that will take the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel embarrassed about using the thing that could replace you. Say more about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it to do half my work, and I'm good at it, but every month the gap between me and the free version gets smaller. I'm like someone selling water next to a tap, because the free version gets closer to my work every month. So I want to be the person who knows what to ask for and which result is rubbish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the progressive side of you, who'd be affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who do this work and can't switch, like the older woman who does bookkeeping for the market stall. I'd want rules and training paid for by the firms that make the tools, not by the people who lose out. I just don't think it's my job to stop the world while I adapt.

say: I'd say it's **exciting** and scary in equal parts.
I'd say freelancers must be more than a **pair of hands**.
think: Captions and simple copy are the work tools do **better each month**.
Soon a café can ask software for **free** and skip my 120.
do: **Shift** from posting to strategy, photos and local events.
**Learn** video editing and basic analytics this term.
**Ask** my tutor about charity communications work.
feel: **Wired**, like standing at the top of a slide.
**Embarrassed** that I'm using the tool that could replace me.
S1.quote: I'm like someone selling water next to a tap, because the free version gets closer to my work every month.
fieldNote: Her own side gig is directly in the line of fire and she **sees** it clearly.
The adaptive reflex is to move up the value chain, not to resist.
Her progressive side worries about people who can't switch, such as a market-stall bookkeeper.

steps.text: Take a video editing short course this term
Pitch cafés on photo and local event packages
Test AI tools on client work and note where they fail
Sign a petition asking firms to fund retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm terrified and excited and I don't know which will win. Two years means I'm in second year and the world changes under me. I'd be reading everything I could, and probably posting too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my degree might not matter and neither might my side business. If AI does any thinking work as well and cheaper, a café wouldn't need me at all, and neither would a lot of employers. I think I'd be seriously frightened for jobs like Mum's later, when robots catch up in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to build something that's mine: a small studio doing local events, photography, maybe a market stall run by people. I'd save everything from the café and not buy a laptop. I'd also ask Mum to talk to the hospital about what they expect, since she's in a hands-on job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hot and cold. I'd feel an adrenaline rush and then a sinking feeling at night. I'd text my best friend Kara every day, just to hear that somebody else is as freaked out as me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be scared for your mum's job when robots catch up. Say more about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's a nurse, so mostly hands-on, which means she's safer until around 2031. But the paperwork that takes her two hours a day would go first, and the hospital might use that to cut staff. I'd tell her to get comfortable with the new systems, because people who help the machine often keep their seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from your friends who aren't using these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to teach them, honestly. Half my course is avoiding the tools, and when it all lands they'll be behind. I'm not saying that to feel superior. I'd rather have a group of friends who are all okay than one who's ahead and lonely.

say: I'd say I'm **terrified and excited** and unsure which wins.
I'd **post** too much and read everything I can.
think: My degree and my side business might **both stop mattering**.
Mum's hospital could use the **paperwork** change to cut staff.
do: **Build** a small local events and photography studio.
**Save** all café money and skip buying a new laptop.
**Teach** friends the tools so nobody is left behind.
feel: **Adrenaline** by day, a sinking feeling at night.
**Comforted** only by daily texts with my friend Kara.
S2.quote: I'd rather have a group of friends who are all okay than one who's ahead and lonely.
fieldNote: Adrenaline and fear **coexist**; she narrates both honestly.
Her worry spreads to her **mother's** hands-on job and the paperwork cuts.
Wants to bring friends along, a progressive, communal reflex.

steps.text: Start a small local events and photo studio
Save all café pay and hold off buying a laptop
Ask Mum what the hospital expects for staff
Run a tools session for friends on my course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a lot of time if you use it, and most people won't. I'd tell my course to stop pretending the tools are cheating and start asking what a degree is for in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel energised. Five years means I graduate with a year to spare and a portfolio of real client work. The scary part is the graduate job I thought I'd get may not be there, so I'd rather go in with something I built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow Brew and Bloom into a proper small business with four or five clients and use the money to learn video and basic code. I'd try an internship at a charity, to learn how big organisations are handling it. And I'd keep my cushion, about three months of rent, no matter what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awake and bouncy. Like I've been given a head start. A bit of guilt, because I'm lucky to be in a flat with friends and a mum who helps, and not everyone can do this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you feel lucky. What would you do with that luck for other people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run a free workshop in the library for older people who run market stalls. They'd be the ones hit hardest and they have the least help. It wouldn't solve anything big, but I'd know a few more people can use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw graduate schemes cancelled or companies freezing hiring in 2029, I'd put more into the side business and less into the degree. I'd also stop spending on trips. I plan with deadlines, so I'm okay changing the plan as the numbers change.

say: I'd say five years is a lot of time if you **use it**.
I'd ask the course what a **degree is for** in 2031.
think: Five years gives me a **portfolio** and a year to spare.
The graduate job I expected may not exist, so I'd **build my own**.
do: **Grow** the café work into four or five small clients.
**Take** a charity internship to see how big groups cope.
**Keep** a three-month rent cushion whatever happens.
feel: **Awake and bouncy**, like I've got a head start.
A little **guilty** about being lucky to have family help.
S3.quote: If I saw graduate schemes cancelled or companies freezing hiring in 2029, I'd put more into the side business and less into the degree.
fieldNote: Plans with **deadlines** and tripwires, so she can switch quickly.
Guilt about her luck turns into a community plan: a free workshop.
Still uneasy because the graduate path itself might vanish.

steps.text: Grow the café work into four or five small clients
Apply for a summer internship at a charity
Keep three months of rent in a savings account
Run a free tools workshop for market stallholders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use ten years to do this properly, and not leave it to a few companies. I'd post about it and say that in ten years my generation will be the ones running things, so our views matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel good. Ten years is a whole working life's first half, almost. I'd be 28 with experience, savings, maybe a small business. It's the one where being adaptive is a real advantage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work part-time in communications, and keep building a client list. I'd learn about data and ethics, because I think those jobs will be needed. And I'd put money aside each month, maybe invest a little, so I'm never in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Light. Hopeful, even. Like knowing a storm is coming but you've got a coat, a boat and a map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said being adaptive is an advantage. Is there a downside to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I jump onto things fast and sometimes drop them just as fast. In ten years I might chase every trend and never get deep at anything. I'd need a friend or a mentor to ask me, what are you actually good at?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And your family in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would be near retirement by 2036. I'd want to help her, maybe pay off some of her rent, and I'd want my life settled enough to do it. The long timeline lets me plan to be the one who helps my mum, instead of being helped.

say: I'd say ten years should be used to do this **properly**.
I'd say my generation will run things, so our **views matter**.
think: Ten years makes **being adaptive** a real advantage.
I could be 28 with **savings** and a small business.
do: **Finish** the degree and work part-time in communications.
**Study** data and ethics, jobs I think will be needed.
**Invest** a small amount monthly so I'm never in panic.
feel: **Hopeful**, like having a coat, a boat and a map.
Slightly **worried** I'd chase trends and never get deep.
S4.quote: The long timeline lets me plan to be the one who helps my mum, instead of being helped.
fieldNote: Self-aware about her **chasing-trends** habit and names a remedy.
Time turns her ambition into **care for her mum**.
Calm is earned by a long runway and family backing, not by being naive.

steps.text: Finish the degree while working part-time in communications
Take data and ethics modules in second year
Invest 30 a month in a low-cost fund
Plan to help Mum with her rent when she retires

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. It's the one where I can't build anything solid before it lands, and where my mum's hospital and the cafés I work for all change at once. What would help is a plan from the government about income, and training that doesn't cost a fortune.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people think young people who use AI all day don't worry. Young people who use AI all day worry quietly, because we're supposed to be the ones who know what's going on. Honestly, I don't.

headlineQuote: Young people who use AI all day worry quietly, because we're supposed to be the ones who know what's going on.
portrait: Iris is an **18-year-old** media and sociology student who runs a café's Instagram and uses AI every day.
She is **adaptive** by habit: she builds side income and tries tools before her friends do.
Her politics lean **progressive**, so she worries about people who can't switch, like her mum's colleagues.
Her cushion is **modest**: 150 from her mum, 120 from the café, and rent that bites after June.
She moves from calm in the quiet world to alarm in 2028, then to hopeful planning when she has ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because nothing solid can be built before it lands and her mother's hospital changes too.
whatWouldHelp: A government **income plan** and cheap training so people aren't left behind.
Honest **advice** from universities on which graduate paths still exist.
